newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 3.

text.p: Data-matching between government departments detected nearly $30 million worth of benefit fraud and overpayments last year and has doubled the number of investigations by Income Support's benefit crime units. The data-matching system, which will cost $13 million of the total benefit crime unit budget of $33 million, is considered one of the most valuable tools in stamping out benefit fraud and overpayment. Page 1.

An independent inquiry into the safety of Christchurch Hospital services would be held, Health Minister Bill English announced at the weekend. The decision comes after staff said the deaths of four patients at the hospital in the last six months were the result of unsafe practices. English announced the inquiry after meeting crown health enterprise board management and staff representatives on Saturday. Page 2.

The Cabinet is expected to take another look today at its decision to grant $4 million extra funding to Maori broadcaster Aotearoa Television Network after allegations about the company's business deals. The grant was halted last week after reports about links between the company and two former European Pacific executives. Page 2.

Cultural projects have been shelved and key arts funding agencies forced to become heavily dependent on lottery funding because the Cultual Affairs Ministry is struggling for cash. Briefing papers prepared by the ministry for Cultural Affairs Minister Christine Fletcher paint a picture of an under-resourced and under-staffed ministry which has enough funding only to manage its core responsibilities. Page 3.

Investors seemed to be indulging in wishful thinking last week when they gave Lion Nathan shares a strong upward nudge as speculation mounted about the future control of the brewer. There was a feeling that a takeover battle was just the medicine the market needed by a market that was going through a dull patch. By Friday, however, Lion Nathan went off the boil and the price eased to $3.75, down 12 cents on the week's high. But this was still comfortably above the $3.20 low recorded last year. On the face of it Lion Nathan looks a perfect takeover target, which is why investors in Australia and New Zealand seem so reluctant to accept assurance that nothing is going on. Page 14.

Telephone service company Telegroups will escalate its assault on the international toll call market with the introduction of cut-price direct dialling from New Zealand in April. The lowa-based communications company is one of several operating in New Zealand offering low-cost international calls through a service known as callback. To use the service callers have to dial a number and then wait to be automatically called back before they can make cut-price calls.
